Recitation is the fifth studio album by Envy, the Japanese band known for fusing post-hardcore/screamo with expansive post-rock. It was released in 2010, with distribution handled by different labels by region (Sonzai in Japan, Rock Action in Europe, and Temporary Residence Ltd. in North America).

High-level profile
- Artist: Envy (Tokyo, Japan)
- Release year: 2010
- Album type: Full-length studio album
- Labels: Sonzai (JP), Rock Action (EU), Temporary Residence Ltd. (NA)
- Language: Japanese (with poetic, often spoken-word/recited vocals)
- Lineup at the time: 
  - Tetsuya Fukagawa – vocals, keys/electronics
  - Nobukata Kawai – guitar
  - Masahiro Tobita – guitar
  - Manabu Nakagawa – bass
  - Dairoku Seki – drums

Sound and style
- Continues Envy’s hallmark blend of emotionally intense hardcore and cinematic post-rock, but places an even greater emphasis on spoken-word “recitation” passages from Tetsuya Fukagawa, with screams and sung parts used more sparingly for impact.
- Long-form songwriting with wide dynamic swings: quiet, shimmering guitar figures and ambient interludes that build into dense, cathartic climaxes.
- Textural, layered guitars and driving, martial drums; melodies lean melancholic-to-hopeful rather than overtly “metallic.”
- The lyrics (in Japanese) read like free-verse poetry—images of memory, time, perseverance, loss, and faint light/hope recurring throughout.

Notable points
- Generally regarded as a maturation of the band’s Insomniac Doze-era direction, leaning further into atmosphere and narrative pacing.
- One of the standout tracks often cited by listeners is Worn Heels and the Hands We Hold, which also received a music video and became a live staple.
- Released on CD, digital, and double LP vinyl editions.
- Received positive critical reception for its emotional scope and arrangements; some noted its length and measured pacing as a deliberate, immersive choice.

Context in Envy’s discography
- Preceded by Insomniac Doze (2006); followed by Atheist’s Cornea (2015) and The Fallen Crimson (2020).
- Sits at a pivotal point where Envy’s screamo roots fully intertwine with spacious, post-rock composition.
